claim.content: A computational procedure is used and validated whereby the calculated Bloch wavefunction $|\phi\rangle$ is projected onto spin and site-resolved orbital bases to compute coefficients $C_{i,l,m,\eta}=\langle\phi|(\varsigma_{\eta}\otimes |l,m\rangle_{ii}\langle l,m|)|\phi\rangle$ and then summed over the atomic sites belonging to a chosen real-space sector; such sector-resolved spin projections reveal that Kramers-degenerate bands can have their two degenerate branches localized on distinct real-space sectors, each carrying opposite spin polarization. Applying this projection enables visualization and quantification of R-2 (compensated Rashba-type) and D-2 (compensated Dresselhaus-type) textures even though the bands remain globally doubly degenerate.

paper:813147782394150913.en_abstract: Spin–orbit coupling can induce spin polarization in nonmagnetic 3D crystals when the inversion symmetry is broken, as manifested by the bulk Rashba and Dresselhaus effects. We establish that these spin-polarization effects originate fundamentally from specific atomic site asymmetries, rather than, as generally accepted, from the asymmetry of the crystal space group. This understanding leads to the recognition that a previously overlooked hidden form of spin polarization should exist in centrosymmetric crystals. Although all energy bands must be doubly degenerate in centrosymmetric materials, we find that the two components of such doubly degenerate bands could have opposite polarizations, each spatially localized on one of the two separate sectors forming the inversion partners. We demonstrate such hidden spin polarizations in particular centrosymmetric crystals by first-principles calculations. This new understanding could considerably broaden the range of currently useful spintronic materials and enable the control of spin polarization by means of operations on the atomic scale.
paper:813147782394150913.en_title: Hidden spin polarization in inversion-symmetric bulk crystals

premises.content: The projection of the Bloch wavefunction onto site-centered atomic orbital basis sets $|l,m\rangle_i$ with the standard Wigner–Seitz radii from the Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package (VASP) projector-augmented wave (PAW) datasets yields spin coefficients $C_{i,l,m,\eta}$ that are quantitatively stable with respect to small changes in the Wigner–Seitz radius values, the choice of PAW dataset, and the set of angular momentum channels included; the sector-summed spin polarization directions and magnitudes are robust to these choices.
premises.metadata: {"weak_types": ["computational", "measurement"], "weakness_reason": "The paper does not report any convergence tests for the projection method. The set of |l,m\u27e9 projectors included in the PAW dataset is fixed; for delocalized states, significant spin density may exist in interstitial regions not captured by any atomic sphere, or in higher angular momentum channels not present in the PAW. The paper acknowledges the need for advanced methods, implying the current approach is provisional.", "failure_mode": "If the sector-resolved spin projection is sensitive to the Wigner\u2013Seitz radius or angular-momentum basis, then the visualizations of opposite spin polarization on \u03b1 and \u03b2 sectors (the key evidence for R-2/D-2) could be quantitatively or even qualitatively unreliable\u2014for example, they could overstate the degree of localization or the direction of the spin vector. The sector-projection method would then not constitute a validated tool for revealing hidden spin textures, weakening the core empirical support for the existence of R-2 and D-2."}

steps.reasoning: Define the calculated Bloch wavefunction $|\phi\rangle$ as the single-particle Kohn–Sham state obtained from density functional theory (DFT) calculations; define an atomic-site orbital basis $|l,m\rangle_{i}$ as the angular-momentum eigenstate with orbital quantum number $l$ and magnetic quantum number $m$ on atomic site $i$; define the spin projector operators $\varsigma_{\eta}$ where $\eta$ labels spin direction components (for example, spin up/down along a chosen axis). The projection coefficient $C_{i,l,m,\eta}$ is defined by the expectation value $C_{i,l,m,\eta} = \langle \phi | (\varsigma_{\eta} \otimes |l,m\rangle_{ii}\langle l,m|) | \phi \rangle$, which yields the contribution of orbital $|l,m\rangle_{i}$ and spin component $\eta$ to the Bloch state $|\phi\rangle$.

Explain that summing $C_{i,l,m,\eta}$ over the set of atomic sites $i$ that belong to a chosen real-space sector (defined as a collection of atoms forming a physically meaningful domain such as a single layer, denoted $\alpha$ or $\beta$) and over orbital indices $l,m$ yields the sector-resolved spin projection for that spin component $\eta$; this summation procedure produces a quantitative measure of how much of the Bloch state's spin character resides on a particular spatial sector. The authors implement this by summing the coefficients for the given spin direction across the atomic sites belonging to the sector.

State that the projection procedure allows one to distinguish the two Kramers-degenerate branches of a doubly-degenerate band by their spatial localization: by applying the projection separately to the two degenerate wavefunctions (or to an orthogonal pair constructed as linear combinations), one can find that one branch localizes predominantly on one real-space sector while the other localizes on the inversion-partner sector, and that these two branches carry opposite spin polarizations when resolved onto those sectors; thus the projection exposes spatially segregated, opposite spin textures even though the bands are globally energetically degenerate. The authors assert this behavior and demonstrate it for specific materials. Fig. 3Fig. 4

Provide the explicit computational context in which this projection is carried out: the band-structure and wavefunctions $|\phi\rangle$ are computed with first-principles DFT using the projector-augmented wave (PAW) method and Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof exchange-correlation functional as implemented in the VASP code; spin-orbit coupling is included via a perturbation term $\sum_{i,l,m} V_{i}^{\text{SO}} \mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{S}\,|l,m\rangle_{ii}\langle l,m|$, where $V_{i}^{\text{SO}}$ is the site-dependent spin-orbit potential and $\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{S}$ is the orbital–spin coupling operator; these methodological details place the projection in a concrete numerical framework. [23][24][25][26][29]

Note that the authors construct atomic orbital projectors using Wigner–Seitz radii from the chosen pseudopotentials (the numerical parameters used to construct $|l,m\rangle_{i}$) and state that in future work they will extend the projection to arbitrary-shaped volumes; this clarifies that the present projections are atomic-site based and rely on the specific PAW projector definitions provided by the computational implementation. [26]

Summarize the methodological conclusion: projecting calculated Bloch wavefunctions onto spin and site-resolved orbital bases by computing $C_{i,l,m,\eta}=\langle \phi | (\varsigma_{\eta} \otimes |l,m\rangle_{ii}\langle l,m|) | \phi \rangle$ and then summing over atomic sites belonging to a chosen real-space sector yields sector-resolved spin projections that reveal whether degenerate bands have their two degenerate branches localized on distinct real-space sectors with opposite spin polarization; this procedure thereby enables visualization and quantification of hidden (compensated) R-2 and D-2 textures even when bands remain globally doubly degenerate. motivating_questions.content: The methodological obstacle was that energetic double degeneracy (enforced by time-reversal and inversion symmetry) typically masks any spin character when one inspects only total-cell-averaged spin expectation values. There was a need for a sector-resolved projection technique that respects the wavefunction structure and reveals hidden, spatially segregated spin polarizations. The described projection procedure resolves that limitation by attributing spin expectation values to physically meaningful real-space sectors composed of groups of atomic sites, thus transforming a formal degeneracy into experimentally and computationally accessible local spin information.
